incidents.title: Celebrity post spike
incidents.brief: A viral post is read 150,000 times in two minutes, but the database is still serving the same row over and over.
incidents.constraint: The content is identical across reads and does not change often.
incidents.question: What is your primary optimization?

choices.label: Deploy Redis Cache-Aside Cluster

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: In-memory caching cuts p95 from 1,800 ms to 120 ms and DB CPU from 92% to 16%. Tradeoff: when the hot key's TTL expires, every request misses at once (cache stampede).

choices.resultBody: The viral post is now served from Redis in about 1 ms per GET; only misses reach Postgres, so DB CPU falls from 92% to 16%. Cost: the key's TTL now decides freshness, and its expiry is a stampede waiting to happen.

choices.label: Deploy PostgreSQL Read Replicas (Read/Write Splitting)

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Spreads SQL query load across read replica nodes. Tradeoff: Asynchronous replication lag creates stale reads on immediate updates.

choices.resultBody: Reads for the post are spread across the replica pool, so primary CPU drops from 92% to 28%. Cost: asynchronous replication means a user who just commented may read a replica that hasn't seen it yet.

choices.label: Increase connection pool to 2,000 sockets without caching

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Each Postgres connection is a process with its own memory; 2,000 of them contending for one hot row add lock and context-switch overhead, not throughput.

choices.resultBody: The hot row already sits in the buffer pool, so disk was never the limit. 2,000 backends now fight over the same row's buffer lock and CPU scheduler; context switching pushes p95 from 1,800 ms to 2,250 ms and errors triple.

hints: The same row is read 150,000 times while it barely changes.
The database is burning CPU re-answering an identical question, not waiting on disk.
Keep a copy of the answer somewhere much cheaper to read than Postgres.

incidents.title: ⚡ Second-Order Outage: Cache Stampede
incidents.brief: Two hours after deploying Redis, the 120-second TTL on the viral post key expired during peak evening traffic. 25,000 concurrent requests all missed simultaneously and dog-piled the primary database.
incidents.constraint: DB CPU spiked back to 96% and DB connection pool is locked under a thundering herd.
incidents.question: How do you mitigate the Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd)?

choices.label: Deploy Distributed Mutex Lock (Singleflight) on cache misses

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: One request per key regenerates it from Postgres while the other ~25,000 wait on the lock (or get the stale copy); waiters add a few ms of latency on each miss.

choices.resultBody: Singleflight lock prevented 25,000 duplicate queries. The cache was repopulated with a single DB read.

choices.label: Deploy Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch algorithm)

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Asynchronous background workers refresh hot keys probabilistically before TTL expires.

choices.resultBody: Hot keys were refreshed shortly before expiry by whichever request drew the early-refresh lottery, so the key never went cold and DB CPU stayed near 20%.

choices.label: Set key TTL to 30 days so it never expires during traffic

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Static infinite TTL consumes Redis memory linearly and leaves stale content permanently.

choices.resultBody: Infinite TTL causes Redis RAM exhaustion when millions of keys accumulate, and edits to the post are never reflected.

hints: Multiple concurrent threads are attempting to recalculate the exact same expired key.
Consider synchronizing access so only one process queries the database on a cache miss (Singleflight/Mutex).
Or consider probabilistically refreshing the key in the background before TTL expires.

incidents.title: ⚡ Second-Order Anomaly: Replication Lag
incidents.brief: Users writing comments or updating their profiles immediately refresh the page, but see old data because asynchronous read replicas have a 650ms replication delay.
incidents.constraint: Users report critical data loss and duplicate submissions on recent updates.
incidents.question: How do you achieve Read-Your-Own-Writes consistency under asynchronous replication?

choices.label: Route user's own reads to the Primary DB for 5s after a write (Sticky Token)

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Guarantees read-your-own-writes for the author, while 99% of passive readers still query the replicas.

choices.resultBody: For 5 seconds after a write, the author's reads go to the primary, which covers the 650 ms lag with room to spare; the other ~99% of readers stay on replicas. Cost: a little extra primary load, and the window must be widened if lag ever grows past 5 s.

choices.label: Convert all read replicas to fully synchronous replication

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Every commit now waits for the slowest replica to confirm; one replica stall or network blip blocks all writes, trading availability for a guarantee only the author needed.

choices.resultTitle: Writes Now Wait on Every Replica
choices.resultBody: Stale reads stopped, but each comment commit now blocks until all replicas acknowledge it: p95 jumps from 180 ms to 465 ms, and when one replica paused for a disk snapshot every write in the system stalled with it.

choices.label: Instruct client apps to wait 1,000ms with a spinner before fetching

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Arbitrary client sleeps do not guarantee replication catch-up and degrade user experience.

choices.resultBody: If replica lag exceeds 1,000ms under high load, the stale read bug returns. Client-side sleeps are not a distributed consistency mechanism.

hints: Asynchronous replication always has some lag. Only the author needs to see their write immediately.
Making every write wait for every replica fixes the author's view by slowing everyone else.
Consider routing only the writing user to the primary for a few seconds after a write (read-your-writes session token).

incidents.title: One Redis shard pegged during flash sale
incidents.brief: ShopNow's flash-sale SKU draws 180,000 reads/s. The Redis cluster is healthy except shard 7, which owns that key: 98% CPU, 420 ms p95, and timeouts spilling onto Postgres.
incidents.constraint: One key always hashes to one slot, so adding shards won't split it, and the sale ends in 40 minutes.
incidents.question: How do you take the single hot key off shard 7?

choices.label: In-process L1 cache on each app node, 1-second TTL
choices.resultTitle: Hot key absorbed in app memory
choices.resultBody: Each of the 60 app nodes now answers the SKU from local memory in well under a microsecond and asks Redis at most once per second, so shard 7 drops from 180,000 to ~60 reads/s. Cost: a price change can take up to 1 s to show on each node, and every node holds its own copy.

choices.label: Reshard the Redis cluster from 12 to 24 nodes
choices.resultBody: Resharding moved the SKU's slot to a fresh node, but all 180,000 reads/s for one key still land on whichever node owns it; slot migration traffic pushed p95 to 600 ms mid-sale.

choices.label: Raise the Redis client timeout from 50 ms to 500 ms
choices.resultBody: Fewer calls time out, but shard 7's single command thread is still at 98%; requests now wait up to 500 ms, app threads pile up behind them, and p95 climbs from 420 ms to 900 ms.

hints: Only one node in the cluster is hot; the others are nearly idle.
Hash slots decide placement, and a single key can never be split across shards.
The hottest reads could be answered before they ever leave the app process.

incidents.title: Scraper 404s hammer the product database
incidents.brief: A scraper cycles the same 2 million guessed product IDs on MarketLane at 25,000 req/s. 95% don't exist, so every request misses Redis and queries Postgres, now at 91% CPU.
incidents.constraint: The scraper rotates through thousands of IPs, so blocking addresses doesn't stick.
incidents.question: How do you stop missing IDs from reaching Postgres?

choices.label: Cache 'not found' results for 10 minutes per missing ID
choices.resultBody: The first lookup of each missing ID stores a small tombstone; revisits in the scraper's 80-second cycle are answered in ~0.5 ms. Postgres CPU falls from 91% to 24%. Cost: ~120 MB of Redis for 2 million tombstones, and the create-product path must delete a tombstone or a new item 404s for up to 10 minutes.

choices.label: Add a Postgres index on the product ID column
choices.resultBody: product_id is the primary key and was already indexed, with each lookup served from memory in well under a millisecond. The cost is 25,000 round-trips and backend wakeups per second, so CPU stays at 90%.

choices.label: Rate-limit each client IP to 100 requests per minute
choices.resultTitle: Rotating IPs slip past the limit
choices.resultBody: The scraper spreads across 3,000 IPs, so each stays under the limit; Postgres load barely moves, while shoppers behind one corporate NAT start getting throttled.

hints: Look at what the cache stores when the database says 'no such row'.
The same missing IDs come back roughly every 80 seconds.
An absence is also an answer that can be remembered.

incidents.title: Old prices shown for minutes after edits
incidents.brief: TicketHub serves 90,000 price reads/s through cache-aside with a 5-minute TTL. After a merchant edits a price, buyers see the old one for minutes and 180 checkouts/min fail on price mismatch.
incidents.constraint: Postgres must stay under 30% CPU, so the TTL can't simply be cut to 1 second.
incidents.question: How do edits reach readers within a second?

choices.label: Delete the key after the DB commit, then reload on miss
choices.resultTitle: Edits visible on the next read
choices.resultBody: The write path commits to Postgres and then issues DEL on that price key; the next read misses once and loads the new price. 200 edits/hour add only ~200 extra DB reads, so CPU stays near 27%. Cost: a slow concurrent reader can still re-cache the old value, so keep a short TTL as a safety net.

choices.label: Update the cache first, then write the database row
choices.resultBody: About 3% of edits fail validation or roll back in Postgres, but the cache already advertises those prices; buyers now check out at prices that were never committed, 40 times a minute.

choices.label: Cut the price TTL from 5 minutes to 1 second
choices.resultBody: Staleness falls to 1 s, but all 50,000 price keys now expire every second; Postgres CPU jumps from 26% to 88% and p95 rises from 45 ms to 400 ms.

hints: The bug lives only in the window between an edit and the TTL expiring.
The write path knows exactly which key just became wrong.
Order matters: touch the cache only after the source of truth has committed.

incidents.title: Members see someone else's account page
incidents.brief: After a perf change, StreamBox caches the /account page in Redis keyed by URL alone. At 40,000 req/s, members report seeing another person's name and billing email.
incidents.constraint: This is a privacy incident: leaks must stop now, without taking /account offline.
incidents.question: What must change about how this response is cached?

choices.label: Put the user ID in the key and mark responses private
choices.resultTitle: Each member gets their own entry
choices.resultBody: Keys become account:{userId} and responses carry Cache-Control: private, so no shared layer can hand one member's page to another. Leaks stop immediately. Cost: hit ratio falls from 99% to ~70% because each entry is reused only by its owner, and DB CPU rises to about 30%.

choices.label: Lower the /account cache TTL from 10 minutes to 5 seconds
choices.resultBody: Leaked pages now live 5 s instead of 10 minutes, but at 40,000 req/s thousands of members still land on someone else's entry in each window, and reports keep arriving.

choices.label: Add Vary: User-Agent so each device type caches separately
choices.resultBody: Varying on User-Agent only splits entries by browser and OS; every Chrome-on-Windows member still shares one /account entry, so leaks continue at about 110 per minute.

hints: The page differs per viewer, but the cache key does not.
Ask what the key must contain so that two different members can never collide.
Shared caches also need to be told that this response belongs to one person.

incidents.title: Database spikes every hour on the hour
incidents.brief: NewsPulse warms 400,000 article keys at 09:00 with a flat 1-hour TTL. At 10:00, 11:00 and 12:00 they expire together and Postgres hits 95% CPU for 90 seconds.
incidents.constraint: Between spikes the hit ratio is 98% and Redis memory is fine; only the synchronized expiry hurts.
incidents.question: How do you stop the keys expiring in lockstep?

choices.label: Add random jitter of plus or minus 10% to each TTL
choices.resultBody: TTLs now land between 54 and 66 minutes, so roughly 550 keys expire per second instead of 400,000 at once, and Postgres peaks at 35%. Cost: freshness is less predictable (some articles live 6 minutes longer), and the keys need one refill cycle to fall out of step.

choices.label: Re-warm all 400,000 keys with a cron job at :59
choices.resultBody: The cron job issues 400,000 DB reads in under a minute and resets every TTL to the same instant, so the 95% spike simply happens at :59 instead of :00.

choices.label: Double the TTL to 2 hours for every article
choices.resultTitle: Half as often, twice as stale
choices.resultBody: Spikes now arrive every two hours instead of every hour, but all 400,000 keys still expire together, and article corrections take up to 2 hours to appear.

hints: The spike happens at the same minute every hour.
Every key was written at the same moment with the same lifetime.
If lifetimes weren't identical, the expiries wouldn't line up.
